summary:
Kiln Watch is a web app that gives one consistent fire record for any place on Earth, from 2000 to today.

The challenge. NASA’s fire hotspots come from MODIS and VIIRS, which count differently. When VIIRS arrived, raw counts jumped several times over, though nothing changed on the ground. We put every satellite on one scale using peer-reviewed methods, and tested the record by switching satellites off and rebuilding it.

Beyond harmonization. A live map shows the harmonized fire record, a burning calendar and a 30-day early warning of unusual conditions, with alerts. We built a kiln detection system, so farmers can see whether a kiln is operating in their area and download the report. A separate exposure page shows which schools, hospitals, clinics and roads sit where fire is seen. News reports are checked against the satellites. An agentic AI analyst and our own MCP server with around 40 tools answer questions from the pipeline’s own numbers.

Why it matters. Fire data is only useful if people can act on it. Early warning tells responders where to prepare before the season peaks. Exposure shows which schools, hospitals and clinics sit there. Farmers can report kilns and plan around the boro harvest.
details:
What it does

Kiln Watch gives one consistent fire record for any place on Earth, 2000 to today. It shows who lives and works where fire is seen, checks news reports against the satellites, and finds likely brick kilns so they are not counted as wildfires. It has seven parts:

  1. Harmonization
  2. Exposure
  3. Early warning and alert
  4. News against satellites
  5. Kiln detection and Boro harvest for Bangladesh
  6. Agentic AI analyst
  7. MCP server

Harmonization

When a sharper satellite (VIIRS) arrived in 2012, raw fire counts jumped several times over, though nothing changed on the ground. We put every satellite (Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) on one scale, Aqua MODIS, so the record stays level across every satellite change. Every value carries an interval, and a switch shows the same record on the VIIRS scale. We tested the method by taking satellites away and rebuilding the record without them.

Exposure

We match every place where satellites see fire to the people, hospitals, clinics, schools, major roads and farmland inside it (WorldPop, OpenStreetMap, ESA WorldCover). Each fire case also gets a verdict from six witnesses: the satellite record, a MODIS-against-VIIRS check, NASA EONET, GDACS, MODIS burned area and the news. Click a cell and see which facilities are there. This is exposure, not damage.

Early warning and alert

For every half-degree cell on Earth, the map shows what the next 30 days usually bring and how unusual the last 30 were. It compares with earlier years and never forecasts. Alerts go out by email or n8n, and can be set for any box on the map. Early warning says where to look, and exposure says which schools and hospitals are there.

News against satellites

We check news and agency reports (NASA EONET, GDACS, GDELT, Google News) against our satellite detections for the same place and month. The reports sit beside the detections on the live map, and each one is marked as seen by both or by one source only. Missing news never means no fire, and a source that could not look says why. Journalists and NGOs can check a headline against the satellites in one view.

Kiln detection and Boro Harvest for Bangladesh

Brick kilns are small, hot and steady, so VIIRS sees them while MODIS mostly cannot, and they can be mistaken for wildfires. We find these persistent heat sources and keep them apart from vegetation fires, so a kiln season never inflates the fire record. Around Dhaka, kilns run from November to April, and each one is labelled a "likely kiln" until it is checked against a kiln inventory. A kiln near the fields hampers the harvest, but until now farmers had no way to prove one was operating there. With Kiln Watch, they can check for one, download the report as proof, report the kiln, and plan around the boro harvest.

Agentic AI analyst

The analyst plans and chains tool calls, pulls the record, news and exposure, draws charts, and moves the map itself. Every tool call is shown to the user. The model writes the words, and every number comes from the pipeline. Any app can call the same analyst through POST /api/agent.

MCP server

Our MCP server at /mcp offers around 40 tools, expert characters and resources. It works with Claude, Cursor and n8n, so any AI assistant or workflow can ask for the fire record, exposure, news and early warning. Every answer comes from the same pipeline the app uses, so the numbers match everywhere.

Benefits and impact

  • Responders: see which hospitals, clinics, schools and villages sit in fire-prone cells before the season peaks.
  • Health and education officials: know which facilities to check after a fire.
  • Farmers: see whether a likely kiln is operating near their fields, download the report, report the kiln, and plan around the boro harvest.
  • Farm agencies: see how much cropland is exposed.
  • Kiln monitoring: brick kilns are kept apart from vegetation fires, so a kiln season is never mistaken for a wildfire season, and each likely kiln is tracked by season.
  • Journalists and NGOs: check a headline against the satellites.
  • Scientists: get a record that survives the end of MODIS, with its uncertainty and provenance.

Locally, in Bangladesh

  • Home test case: Dhaka's brick-kiln belt is where raw counts mislead most. Kilns are small, hot and steady, so VIIRS sees them and MODIS mostly cannot. Raw counts there show a false 10.6-times jump, and in our tests the error for Dhaka falls from +1864% uncalibrated to +13% harmonized.
  • Kiln detection: we find likely kilns around Dhaka, active from November to April, and keep them apart from vegetation fires. They are labelled "likely kilns" until they are checked against a kiln inventory.
  • Farmers: a farmer can check whether a likely kiln is operating in their area, download the report, and report a kiln. The kiln season overlaps the boro rice season, so farmers can plan around the boro harvest.
  • Exposure: wherever fire has been seen around Dhaka, we match the schools, hospitals, clinics and major roads, and the people and cropland around them. Click a cell and see which facilities are there.
  • Early warning: the 30-day outlook covers Bangladesh, and alerts can be set for any box in the country.
  • News against satellites: we check news and agency reports (NASA EONET, GDACS, GDELT, Google News) against our satellite detections for the same place and month. Each report is marked as seen by both, or by one source only. Missing news never means no fire, and a source that could not look says why.

Creative

  • Live map: the harmonized record, the burning calendar and the 30-day outlook in one place, with a list of places to watch.
  • Live map, news: reports beside the satellite detections for the same place and month.
  • Exposure page: schools, hospitals and clinics where fire was seen, in one click.
  • Kiln detection: likely kilns kept apart from vegetation fires, with a report farmers can download.
  • MCP server: around 40 tools, expert characters and resources, at /mcp, for Claude, Cursor and n8n.
  • AI API: POST /api/agent, an analyst any app can call.
  • Agentic AI: the analyst plans and chains tool calls, pulls the record, news and exposure, draws charts, and moves the map itself. Every tool call is shown. The model writes the words, and every number comes from the pipeline.

Tools

  • Code: Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, React, MapLibre and three.js.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS, GIBS, Black Marble and EONET, plus Sentinel, GDACS, GDELT, WorldPop and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hosting: Docker, GitHub Actions, Azure Container Apps and Vercel.
  • AI: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus (via Claude Code) by Anthropic, and Gemini Argon and Gemini Flash by Google, for planning and development. Gemini 2.5 Flash for the in-app analyst.
  • Hardware: none.

Factors our team considered

  • Science-backed harmonization: every step comes from peer-reviewed papers. The fire products follow Schroeder et al. and Giglio et al. The calibration uses Efron & Morris (empirical Bayes), DerSimonian & Laird and Frost & Thompson (regression dilution). The intervals follow Lei et al. (conformal prediction), and the trends follow Sen.
  • Planning and judging ideas: we compared our plans and ideas against top AI models (Claude Fable, Claude Opus, Gemini Argon) before building.
  • Checking: we used agentic AI skills to check every feature and its working, more than once.
  • Satellite scale: Aqua, the only satellite flown continuously from 2002.
  • Open limits: scan-angle effects and sensor-only hotspots are measured, and cloud cover is still open.
  • Reproducibility: every file records its data versions and code version.
  • Honest wording: detections are not fires, exposure is context, not impact, and kilns are "likely kilns" until checked against an inventory.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Planning: Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic) and Gemini Argon (Google) helped us read the challenge brief, review the literature and rules, and design the method (Aqua MODIS as the reference sensor, satellite-denial tests, accessibility). They worked only on public material: the challenge page, published papers, and NASA/NOAA documentation.
  • Code: Claude Opus through Claude Code (Anthropic) and Gemini Flash (Google) helped write and review the code: the data pipeline, the harmonization statistics, the API, the MCP server and the web app. They also ran builds and tests. They worked on our own source code and on public NASA FIRMS fire detections. This code is acknowledged as SI-assisted in our repository README and commit metadata.
  • Inside the app: an optional analyst uses Gemini 2.5 Flash (free tier) to put the results of fixed, deterministic tool calls into words. It only sees our pipeline's output, which is built from NASA FIRMS data, and every tool call is shown to the user. Text written by the analyst is SI-generated.
  • Numbers and data: no SI system produces any number in our calendars, charts or downloads. Every number comes from our open pipeline run on NASA FIRMS data. We gave no personal or private data to any SI tool, and the team reviewed all code and results. No SI-generated content uses or modifies NASA logos, flags, or other branding.
